newsitem.title: FRANCE: Communists see Jospin hint of euro consultation.
newsitem.headline: Communists see Jospin hint of euro consultation.

text.p: The French Communist party welcomed on Friday a remark by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin it said might mean he would consult the people before joining a single European currency.

In his first television interview since taking office, Jospin said on Thursday that if the government had to make a choice between qualifying for the single currency and preserving economic growth, he would put the issue to the country.

"We will try to define a path which takes account of these contradictory factors," Jospin said. "If there has to be a choice in one direction rather than the other, we...will present the issues of this choice to the country and by its reaction, its indications, it will help us decide."

He did not spell out how the country would be expected to make its preference known and political analysts questioned whether Jospin was really hinting at a referendum, which would require conservative President Jacques Chirac's agreement.
The prime minister immediately added: "In any case, it will be our responsibility to take the decisions. But we will do it without hiding anything or manipulating anything, by telling the truth."
Communist parliamentary floor leader Alain Bocquet said Jospin had given citizens room to have their say, although he had not understood exactly what the prime minister meant.

"I didn't precisely hear the word referendum, but it seems to me absolutely indispensible to consult the French people before the European challenges and choices of tomorrow," he told Radio Luxembourg.

The Communist party, junior partner in Jospin's left-wing coalition, was long hostile to European economic and monetary union and campaigned for a referendum on the euro in this year's parliamentary election.
Jospin opposed such a move, saying the French people had approved the Maastricht treaty on European union by referendum in September 1992 and France had given its word.
Under the constitution, the president may, upon the proposal of the government or a joint proposal by both houses of parliament, submit a law, treaty or decision to a referendum.

The constitutional scope for such consultations was enlarged by a 1995 amendment which allowed for referendums on "reforms relating to the economic or social policy of the nation and of public services".
